encounters.cc: Recurrent infections including otitis media, sinusitis, and pneumonia since early childhood.

lines: Recurrent infections including otitis media, sinusitis, and pneumonia since early childhood.
Since early childhood, he has suffered from repeated episodes of otitis media, sinusitis, and two hospitalizations for pneumonia.
He also had an episode of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia requiring prolonged therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
His parents report that he fails to thrive compared to his siblings, with poor weight gain and frequent loose stools.
Vaccination history is up to date, but he has not developed protective titers against encapsulated bacteria despite multiple immunizations.
Past medical history is otherwise unremarkable.
- Pancrelipase 3 capsules with meals and snacks
- Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg TMP PO daily (PCP prophylaxis)
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg PO twice daily
- Antiretroviral therapy Age-appropriate combination therapy per pediatric HIV protocol
- Maintenance chemotherapy for ALL Per current oncology protocol
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Elementary school student.
On physical examination, the child appears thin and mildly pale with small, firm cervical lymph nodes.

lines: Six-month history of increasing fatigue, abdominal distension, easy bruising, and frequent epistaxis.

His parents report that he often appears ill during these episodes, with reduced appetite and occasional vomiting.
He has met all developmental milestones.

On examination today, the child is afebrile but appears thin and mildly pale.
Abdominal exam reveals no organomegaly, but there is mild costovertebral angle tenderness.
Laboratory studies show normocytic anemia and elevated serum creatinine.
Urinalysis reveals leukocyte esterase and nitrites, and urine culture grows Escherichia coli .
Renal ultrasound demonstrates asymmetric kidney size with focal areas of cortical thinning bilaterally.
A voiding cystourethrogram is planned for further evaluation.

lines: Recurrent episodes of fever, abdominal pain, and dysuria over the past year despite antibiotic therapy.

His parents report that he has been treated with antibiotics for urinary tract infections on four separate occasions, and each time his symptoms resolved temporarily before recurring a few months later.
His growth and development are normal, and he is otherwise healthy.

lines: Several weeks of increasing fatigue, reduced energy, headaches, and difficulty seeing the classroom chalkboard.

His appetite has also declined, and his parents have noticed that his shoes and clothes still fit him the same despite his classmates outgrowing theirs.

lines: Six-month history of recurrent infections including otitis media, pneumonia, and a recent episode of herpes zoster.

He has had multiple episodes of otitis media, two episodes of pneumonia, and a recent case of herpes zoster.

His mother died two years ago from complications of a chronic illness.
He is brought to the clinic by his grandmother
Physical examination today reveals palpable lymph nodes in the right axilla and mild hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory tests reveal mild anemia and a normal neutrophil count.

encounters.cc: Chronic fatigue, difficulty walking, and frequent bone pain over the past 6 months despite pancreatic enzyme replacement.

lines: Chronic fatigue, difficulty walking, and frequent bone pain over the past 6 months despite pancreatic enzyme replacement.

The patient is a 10-year-old male with cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency, previously evaluated in this department for Gaucher disease and craniopharyngioma, who returns for assessment of persistent malabsorptive and musculoskeletal symptoms.
His mother reports that he continues to have frequent bulky, foul-smelling stools that float in the toilet bowl, despite adherence to pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy.
She notes that his stools are difficult to flush and often leave an oily film in the water.
Over the past 6 months, he has been complaining of aching in his legs, especially after running, and difficulty climbing stairs.
She has also noticed that he seems to tire more easily than other children his age and prefers sedentary activities such as drawing instead of outdoor play.
The child was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 2 after recurrent respiratory infections and failure to thrive prompted genetic testing, which confirmed a mutation in the CFTR gene.

Since that time, he has required repeated hospitalizations for pneumonia, most commonly with Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and is on a regimen of inhaled antibiotics, bronchodilators, and chest physiotherapy.
- Pancrelipase 3 capsules with meals and snacks
- Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg TMP PO daily (PCP prophylaxis)
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg PO twice daily
- Antiretroviral therapy Age-appropriate combination therapy per pediatric HIV protocol
- Maintenance chemotherapy for ALL Per current oncology protocol
His family history is significant for an older sibling who also has cystic fibrosis and required a lung transplant at age 15.
His parents are non-consanguineous and healthy.
The child lives in a suburban home with his family and attends school regularly, but has missed several days due to illness.
On review of systems, the mother adds that he has had poor appetite, irritability, and occasional abdominal bloating.
She denies recent trauma but is concerned that he may have nutritional deficiencies.
He has not had any seizures or syncope.
On examination, his height is at the 5th percentile and weight at the 3rd percentile for age.
He appears thin with minimal subcutaneous fat.
His sclerae are anicteric, but there is generalized pallor.
The chest shows mild pectus excavatum with scattered crackles bilaterally on auscultation.
The abdomen is soft but mildly distended.
His extremities are thin, and he walks with a slightly waddling gait.
There is tenderness to palpation over the shins and femurs.
Neurologic examination reveals normal cranial nerves, intact sensation, but mild proximal muscle weakness.
Deep tendon reflexes are present and symmetric.
Laboratory evaluation reveals hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
A DEXA scan shows decreased bone mineral density consistent with rickets/osteomalacia.

lines: Acute onset of dyspnea and chest pain following central venous catheter flushing.

Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air.
Physical examination reveals a pale and anxious child with jugular venous distention.
Auscultation of the lungs is clear, and heart sounds are distant.
The CVC site appears unremarkable without signs of infection.
His complete blood count shows a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, leukocytes of 3,000/mm³, and platelets of 75,000/mm³.
